records.title: Need for a national policy and screening framework on maternal mental health.
details:
Smt. Sudha Murty:
?I seek to bring to the attention of the Government an
essential yet frequently overlooked dimension of healthcare, Maternal Mental
Health. Studies show that nearly 1 in 5 new mothers in India experience
Postpartum Depression (PPD). Despite how common this is, mental health issues
after childbirth are rarely spoken about. Most women suffer in silence, which
can lead to severe emotional distress, difficulty bonding with the baby,
chronic physical exhaustion, and long-term delays in a childs cognitive growth.
While our healthcare system has done wonderful work in significantly reducing
the maternal mortality rate, mental health needs equal attention. A simple and
successful model already exists in Karnataka, where mental health checks are
part of the Thayi Card Scheme. Frontline ASHA workers are trained to use a
short questionnaire designed by NIMHANS to screen for early signs of depression
during home visits. When it is identified that a mother needs help, she is
immediately referred to medical officers at local Primary Health Centres or
connected to tele-counseling support.
I humbly request the Government, to create a National Policy on Maternal Mental
Health. We should expand Karnataka?s questionnaire and referral model across
the entire country through the Mother and Child Protection Card. Training our
ASHA workers to recognise these early warning signs will ensure that every new
mother receives timely care, support, and empathy.
(ENDS)

records.title: Need for a national-level scientific probe and awareness campaign on the safe use of weight-loss drugs.
details:
Smt. Sudha Murty: 
I seek to bring to the attention of the
Government a new development in our healthcare sector. In March 2026, the
patents for popular diabetic drugs also used for weight loss, like Ozempic and
Mounjaro, expired in India. Many Indian pharmaceutical companies have already
entered the market to produce these medicines. As a result, these drugs are
becoming significantly cheaper, with some now available at nearly 50% of their
previous price. While it is good that medicine is becoming affordable, we must
also be careful. In a price-sensitive market like India, the sudden mass
availability could lead to widespread misuse for weight loss, without adequate
medical supervision. Clinical studies across the World have linked these
medications to side effects ranging from gastrointestinal distress to rarer,
severe conditions like pancreatitis, gallbladder issues, and potential muscle
loss. I request that the Government, through the ICMR (Indian Council of
Medical Research) and CDSCO (Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation),
initiate a formal, large-scale scientific probe to monitor the long-term impact
of these drugs on the Indian population. We should lead a strong public
awareness campaign to educate our citizens. People need to know that these are
medical treatments, not simple lifestyle products. I also request that the
Government issue clear safety guidelines for healthcare providers. Our goal
must be to ensure that these new medical breakthroughs help improve lives
without causing any unintended health problems.
(ENDS)

records.title: Concern over rising cases of PCOS in Adolescent Girls.
details:
Smt. Sudha Murty: I draw attention of the
Government to a growing but largely neglected health concern affecting
adolescent girls in our country, the Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, or PCOS.PCOS is
commonly understood as a condition affecting adult women. However, research
shows that the pooled prevalence of PCOS among Indian adolescent girls is high,
approximately one in five. A significant proportion of teenage girls are at
risk at a very early stage of life.However, the challenge is that the PCOS
diagnosis in adolescents is delayed until serious complications emerge.
Symptoms such as irregular menstrual cycles, acne, weight gain, or mood swings
are considered normal pubertal changes. If not identified and managed early,
PCOS can lead to long-term metabolic, reproductive, and mental health
consequences, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risks, infertility,
anxiety, and depression. India currently lacks national guidelines specifically
focused on the diagnosis and management of PCOS in young girls. There is also
no systematic mechanism for screening, counselling, or lifestyle guidance
within school health services.Early lifestyle interventions focused on
nutrition, physical activity, and mental well-being have been shown to reduce
the severity and long-term impact of PCOS significantly. I humbly urge the
Government to consider integrating PCOS awareness and early intervention into
existing adolescent health programmes, developing age-appropriate national
guidelines, and strengthening lifestyle education in schools and community
health settings.Early action will protect the health of young girls and
contribute to a healthier future generation.
(ENDS)

records.title: Need for a mandatory national legal framework to address bullying and cyberbullying in schools.
details:
Smt. Sudha Murty: I draw attention of the
Government towards the serious issue of bullying and cyberbullying among school
children. Recent tragedies across the country have shown that this is not just
a personal matter between children but a failure of institutional
accountability. The PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 report by NCERT highlights
the scale of this crisis. It reveals that 32% of students in Indian schools are
teased or mocked, 24% face physical pushing or hitting, and 22% are threatened
by their peers. Alarmingly, only 45% of students find it comfortable to talk to
someone when they feel upset. Despite these figures, only 70% of schools have
reported having an anti-bullying policy in place. While the National Education
Policy 2020 emphasizes mental health, many schools still lack the necessary
counsellors. The Manodarpan tele-helpline has already extended guidance to over
3.2 lakh calls, which clearly indicates the immense psychological needs of our
students. However, a helpline is a support tool, not a substitute for on-ground
safety. Currently, there are only advisory guidelines from the National
Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the Ministry of Education.
Because there is no mandatory national law, implementation is inconsistent
across different States and school boards. I humbly request the Government to
enact a mandatory national framework that includes emotional sensitivity
training in the curriculum and clear and time-bound reporting mechanisms. Every
school must be legally obligated to provide a safe and dignified environment to
fulfil our commitment to the welfare of our children.
(ENDS)
